Biodiesel has also seen an increase in use as a marine fuel in recent years, with numerous vessel operators and ports trialing the use of B100 in place of heavy fuel oil (see Section 2.9). Biodiesel use in the home heating oil market has been increasing in recent years. In 2023, commercial and residential heating accounted for nearly 5% of total U.S. biodiesel consumption, up from roughly 1% a decade earlier (EIA 2025p). The home heating oil market is concentrated in the Northeast. Biodiesel blended with home heating oil is marketed as Bioheat fuel by the National Oilheat Research Alliance.11 B20 can be used in standard home heating oil equipment. 2.7 Ethanol Ethanol is a widely used biofuel made predominantly from corn. Ethanol has a long history of use in the United States, dating back to the introduction of motor vehicles. As a domestically produced biofuel, ethanol provides jobs in rural areas. The ethanol market has expanded to be the largest (by joule) alternative fuel in the United States due to both market factors and policies 10 Clean Fuels Alliance America original equipment manufacturer information: cleanfuels.org/wp- content/uploads/OEM-Support-Summary_Sept-2025.pdf. 11 The National Oilheat Research Alliance provides details on renewable fuels for home heating oil: noraweb.org. 23 This report is available at no cost from the National Laboratory of the Rockies at www.nlr.gov/publications. snoitatS leseidoiB (Johnson et al. 2021). Today, ethanol consumption is driven by both octane requirements and the RFS. Pipelines ship a variety of gasoline and gasoline blendstocks to meet demand, which varies regionally. Many of these products are sub-octane, meaning they have a lower octane than is required for sale to consumers at a station. Ethanol has a higher octane number than gasoline, and refiners provide a gasoline blendstock that, when blended with ethanol, will meet octane specifications necessary for vehicle performance needs. Ethanol is delivered to terminals or blenders by railcar, tanker truck, or barge, and it is then blended with gasoline and delivered by truck to stations. In the United States, 98% of gasoline sold contains ethanol, and nearly all ethanol is sold as E10 (Alternative Fuels Data Center 2025a). Another long-available blend is E85, which can be used in flexible-fuel vehicles. E15 is approved for use in model year 2001 and newer vehicles, which represent 97% of the light-duty gasoline vehicle market.12 The blend rate of ethanol with gasoline reached 10.4% in 2024—this means that the market expanded beyond E10 with sales of E15 and E85 (RFA 2025b). In states without a reformulated gasoline market, E15 typically cannot be sold in summer months due to a waiver needed for Reid vapor pressure. However, an ongoing EPA emergency fuel waiver has allowed sales of E15 nationwide year-round in 2022 and 2023 (EPA 2025c).
